title: Casting an unrepresentable float, float-like string, or `NAN` now warns
summary: PHP 8.5 emits a warning when a float (or a string that looks like a float) is cast to `int` and cannot be represented as one, and separately when `NAN` is cast to any other type; verified directly, both are silent today - `(int) 1.0e30` already returns a meaningless wrapped value (`int(5076964154930102272)`, not an error and not a saturation to `PHP_INT_MAX`) and `(int) NAN` already returns `int(0)` - so the PHP 8.5 warning adds a diagnostic to an existing, unchanged silent miscomputation rather than changing which number comes out.
new_code_policy: Never cast a float, a float-like numeric string, or `NAN`/`INF`/`-INF` to `int` without first checking whether the value can actually be represented as one - `is_finite($x) && $x >= PHP_INT_MIN && $x <= PHP_INT_MAX` before `(int) $x`, not `(int) $x` followed by hoping the result looks sane. This applies to implicit int coercions too - an array offset, a string offset, a `%d`/`%u` conversion in `sprintf()`/`printf()` - not only to an explicit `(int)` cast; anywhere a float-typed or float-like value crosses into an int-only context, validate its range first. When a value might legitimately be out of range (unbounded user input, an untrusted external number), reject or clamp it explicitly and say why, rather than letting the cast silently manufacture a number.
existing_code_policy: Search for `(int)` casts, and int-typed parameters or return types, whose operand is a `float` (or a numeric string that could hold a float-like value) not already known to be in range - unvalidated user input, a computed ratio or sum, a value parsed from an external source. Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19: `(int) 1.0e30` returns `int(5076964154930102272)` - not `PHP_INT_MAX`, not an error, a number with no relationship to `1.0e30` beyond sharing a bit pattern with it - and `(int) -1.0e30` returns the mirror-image `int(-5076964154930102272)`; `(int) NAN` returns `int(0)`; `(int) INF` and `(int) -INF` both also return `int(0)`. A float cast is not the only way to reach this: `(int) (float) PHP_INT_MAX` - casting `PHP_INT_MAX` itself through a float round-trip, since a 64-bit double cannot exactly represent it - returns `int(-9223372036854775808)`, i.e. `PHP_INT_MIN`, demonstrating that even an in-range-looking value can flip to the opposite sign purely from float-precision loss before the int cast ever runs. A numeric string is not guaranteed to agree with the equivalent float literal: `(int) '1.0e30'` (a string) returns `int(9223372036854775807)`, i.e. `PHP_INT_MAX` - a *different* wrong answer than `(int) 1.0e30` (the float literal) produces, because PHP's string-to-int conversion saturates at the `int` boundary while its float-to-int conversion wraps; do not assume a string-typed and a float-typed unrepresentable value fail the same way. Where existing code casts a float or float-like string to `int` without a prior range check, add one (`is_finite($x) && $x >= PHP_INT_MIN && $x <= PHP_INT_MAX`) and decide explicitly what happens when it fails - reject the input, clamp it, or propagate an error - rather than keeping the bare cast. Do not "fix" this by swapping in a clamp (`max(PHP_INT_MIN, min(PHP_INT_MAX, $x))`) without checking whether the call site can also receive `NAN` - `is_finite(NAN)` is `false`, so a `is_finite()` guard already covers it, but a naive `min()`/`max()`-only clamp does not reliably reject `NAN` and needs the explicit finiteness check too.
guideline: Never cast a float, a float-like string, or `NAN`/`INF`/`-INF` to `int` - explicitly or implicitly (array offsets, string offsets, `sprintf('%d', ...)`, an int-typed parameter) - without first confirming the value is finite and within `[PHP_INT_MIN, PHP_INT_MAX]`. An out-of-range or non-finite value produces a number with no meaningful relationship to the original today, silently, and PHP 8.5 only adds a warning on top of that same silent miscomputation - it does not make the result meaningful. Check the value before casting; do not cast and hope.
details: UPGRADING-8.5.0 lists two adjacent entries under Backward Incompatible Changes -> Core, covered together here on the same one-rule-for-a-shared-theme precedent as `core.chr_ord_byte_range` (two adjacent UPGRADING entries) and `core.assert_options` (a function plus five related constants): "A warning is now emitted when casting floats (or strings that look like floats) to int if they cannot be represented as one. This affects explicit int casts and implicit int casts." and "A warning is now emitted when casting NAN to other types." Both are the same underlying mistake - converting a value that has no meaningful integer representation and silently getting a number anyway - on the two ends of the same problem (an unrepresentable magnitude, and the one float value, `NAN`, that has no ordering or magnitude at all). Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19, with `set_error_handler()` installed throughout so any diagnostic PHP raised would print: `(int) 1.0e30` gives `int(5076964154930102272)`, and `(int) -1.0e30` gives `int(-5076964154930102272)` - a sign-mirrored wraparound, not a clamp to `PHP_INT_MAX`/`PHP_INT_MIN` and not an error; `(int) NAN` gives `int(0)`; `(int) INF` and `(int) -INF` both also give `int(0)`, confirming the "no meaningful value" case collapses to `0` rather than to a sentinel or an error. `(string) NAN` gives `"NAN"`, `(bool) NAN` gives `true`, and `(array) NAN` gives `[0 => NAN]` - each silent, demonstrating UPGRADING's "to other types" (plural) scope directly rather than only the int case. The float-vs-string distinction matters and was verified directly: `(int) '1.0e30'` (a numeric string) gives `int(9223372036854775807)`, exactly `PHP_INT_MAX` - a different wrong answer from `(int) 1.0e30` (the float literal), because PHP's string-to-number-to-int path saturates at the int boundary while its float-to-int path performs a raw wraparound; a rule or a fix that assumes these two "look the same" cases fail identically would itself be wrong. Precision loss can also flip an in-range-looking value's sign with no explicit large literal in sight: `(int) (float) PHP_INT_MAX` - `PHP_INT_MAX` is not exactly representable as a 64-bit double, so the round trip through `float` already corrupts it - gives `int(-9223372036854775808)`, i.e. `PHP_INT_MIN`; and a float just past `PHP_INT_MAX` (`(float) PHP_INT_MAX + 1024.0`, which prints as `9.223372036854776E+18` since the addition is itself absorbed by float precision loss) casts to the identical `PHP_INT_MIN`. UPGRADING states the new warning "affects explicit int casts and implicit int casts," so several implicit sites were measured directly rather than assumed to behave like the explicit cast: an array offset, `$arr[1.0e30] = 'x';`, already raises `E_DEPRECATED` (`errno=8192`) with the message "Implicit conversion from float 1.0E+30 to int loses precision" on PHP 8.4.19 - a real, pre-existing diagnostic, but the *wrong* one to credit to this rule, because the identical message and error level were confirmed to also fire for `$arr[3.7] = 'frac';` (an ordinary, perfectly in-range fractional float) - so this existing deprecation is a general precision-loss notice unrelated to the specific unrepresentable-magnitude problem UPGRADING's new PHP 8.5 warning targets, and it was already firing, unchanged, long before 8.5; `$arr[NAN] = 'y';` raises the same existing `E_DEPRECATED` ("Implicit conversion from float NAN to int loses precision") and silently stores under key `0`, while a genuinely clean control case, `$arr[3.0] = 'whole';` (in range, no fractional part), raises nothing at all. A second implicit site, `sprintf('%d', 1.0e30)`, gives the string `"5076964154930102272"` - matching the explicit cast's wrapped value exactly - with **no** diagnostic of any kind, not even the pre-existing array-offset deprecation; `sprintf('%d', NAN)` likewise silently gives `"0"`. A third implicit site is the sharpest contrast measured: passing an unrepresentable float directly to an `int`-typed parameter - `function wantsInt(int $n): int { return $n; }` called as `wantsInt(1.0e30)` or `wantsInt(NAN)`, in a file with no `declare(strict_types=1)`, i.e. ordinary weak-mode coercion - throws `TypeError: wantsInt(): Argument #1 ($n) must be of type int, float given` immediately, today, on PHP 8.4.19; the built-in `intdiv()` was confirmed to behave identically (`intdiv(1.0e30, 2)` and `intdiv(NAN, 2)` both throw the equivalent `TypeError` naming `intdiv()`'s own `$num1` parameter). The same weak-mode coercion at an *in-range* fractional float succeeds instead of throwing - `wantsInt(3.7)` raises the pre-existing `E_DEPRECATED` "Implicit conversion from float 3.7 to int loses precision" and returns `int(3)`, and `wantsInt(3.0)` (whole, in range) succeeds with no diagnostic at all - so this specific implicit site (a typed parameter under weak coercion) is, uniquely among every site measured here, already loud rather than silent for the exact case this rule is about; that existing `TypeError` is not part of what PHP 8.5's new warning changes, and this rule's guidance to check the value before casting is aimed principally at the sites that stay silent - explicit `(int)` casts, array/string offsets, and `sprintf()` - rather than at typed-parameter boundaries, which were already protected. A fourth implicit site, reading a string by a float offset (`$s[1.0e30]` on `$s = 'hello world';`), raises two pre-existing `E_WARNING` (`errno=2`) diagnostics - "String offset cast occurred" and "Uninitialized string offset 5076964154930102272" - and returns `""`; both warnings are general string-offset-coercion diagnostics that also fire for any non-integer offset (they are not specific to unrepresentable magnitudes), but the second one's message happens to expose the same mangled wraparound value seen in the array-offset and `sprintf()` cases. Taken together: PHP already has scattered, inconsistent protection against this class of mistake - a hard `TypeError` at typed-parameter boundaries, an unrelated but overlapping `E_DEPRECATED` at array offsets and string-offset `E_WARNING`s that both predate and are wider in scope than this specific problem, and total silence at a bare `(int)` cast, at `sprintf()`, and (for the string-vs-float divergence) between an out-of-range numeric string and an out-of-range float literal - and PHP 8.5's new warning is aimed squarely at closing the silent gaps, not at replacing the diagnostics that already exist. `introduced_in` is set to "8.5" here because that is the minor the new warnings actually start firing in - the field exists so this behavior_change rule can be range-gated on the feature axis, and it is not a claim that PHP 8.5 introduced int casts, float-to-int conversion, or `NAN` itself, all of which have existed since PHP's earliest versions. On a policy whose entire targeted range sits below 8.5 (for example `8.2.*`), this rule is out of range and does not apply: no PHP runtime in that range warns on these casts, so surfacing the rule there would tell an agent to expect a diagnostic that cannot fire. The silently-wrong values documented here - the wrapped/saturated/zeroed results measured above - are not themselves new at 8.5 and hold on every PHP version this catalog tracks, before and after, but the rule's actionable claim is specifically about the new PHP 8.5 warnings, and gating on `introduced_in` keeps that claim honest for a project that never reaches 8.5. PHPCompatibility was probed directly (2026-09-05) against files covering every case above (explicit casts, the string/float divergence, the boundary and just-past-boundary cases, the array-offset controls, `sprintf()`, weak-mode typed-parameter coercion, `intdiv()`, and the string-offset case) at testVersion 8.2-8.5 and produced zero findings: this is a warning keyed on a runtime numeric value's magnitude, not a function/constant/syntax availability fact, so it sits outside what PHPCompatibility's sniffs are built to detect; `verification.phpcompatibility` is intentionally empty rather than guessed.

after: throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Price out of representable range: {$priceInDollars}");
throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Weight out of representable range: {$rawWeight}");

notes: Verified on PHP 8.4.19 (explicit casts, `set_error_handler()` installed, zero diagnostics for any of these): `(int) 1.0e30` = `int(5076964154930102272)`; `(int) -1.0e30` = `int(-5076964154930102272)`; `(int) NAN` = `int(0)`; `(int) INF` = `int(0)`; `(int) -INF` = `int(0)`; `(string) NAN` = `"NAN"`; `(bool) NAN` = `true`; `(array) NAN` = `[0 => NAN]`; `(int) '1.0e30'` (numeric string, not float literal) = `int(9223372036854775807)` = `PHP_INT_MAX` - a different wrong answer than the float literal's wraparound, because string-to-int saturates while float-to-int wraps; `(int) (float) PHP_INT_MAX` = `int(-9223372036854775808)` = `PHP_INT_MIN`, and a float just past `PHP_INT_MAX` (`(float) PHP_INT_MAX + 1024.0`, printing as `9.223372036854776E+18`) casts to the same `PHP_INT_MIN`. Commands run: `php -l rule7_numeric_casts.php` then `php rule7_numeric_casts.php`.

Verified on PHP 8.4.19 (implicit sites): `$arr[1.0e30] = 'x';` raises pre-existing `E_DEPRECATED` (`errno=8192`) "Implicit conversion from float 1.0E+30 to int loses precision" and stores under key `5076964154930102272`; `$arr[NAN] = 'y';` raises the same `E_DEPRECATED` ("...float NAN...") and stores under key `0`. Controls: `$arr[3.7] = 'frac';` (in-range fractional) raises the *identical* `E_DEPRECATED` message pattern, showing this existing deprecation is a general precision-loss notice, not specific to unrepresentable magnitudes; `$arr[3.0] = 'whole';` (in-range, no fractional part) raises nothing. `sprintf('%d', 1.0e30)` = `"5076964154930102272"` and `sprintf('%d', NAN)` = `"0"`, both with zero diagnostics of any kind - a silent site with no pre-existing protection at all. Reading a string by a float offset, `$s[1.0e30]` on `$s = 'hello world'`, raises two pre-existing `E_WARNING` (`errno=2`) diagnostics, "String offset cast occurred" and "Uninitialized string offset 5076964154930102272", and returns `""`. Commands run: `php -l rule7b_weak_mode.php` then `php rule7b_weak_mode.php` (array-offset and weak-mode-coercion cases); a separate one-off `php -r` invocation for the string-offset read.

Verified on PHP 8.4.19 (weak-mode typed-parameter coercion, no `declare(strict_types=1)`): `wantsInt(1.0e30)` and `intdiv(1.0e30, 2)` both throw `TypeError: ...must be of type int, float given` immediately; `wantsInt(NAN)` and `intdiv(NAN, 2)` throw the identical shape of `TypeError`. By contrast, `wantsInt(3.7)` (in-range fractional) succeeds, raising only the pre-existing `E_DEPRECATED` "loses precision" notice and returning `int(3)`, and `wantsInt(3.0)` (in-range, whole) succeeds with no diagnostic. This is the one site measured here that is already loud, today, for exactly the unrepresentable-value case this rule is about - unlike the bare `(int)` cast, the array offset, and `sprintf()`, all of which stay silent or only carry the unrelated precision-loss deprecation.

PHPCompatibility 10.0.0-alpha2 was run directly (2026-09-05) against files covering the explicit-cast, string/float-divergence, boundary, array-offset-control, `sprintf()`, weak-mode-coercion, `intdiv()`, and string-offset cases above, at testVersion 8.2-8.5, and produced zero findings (`{"errors": 0, "warnings": 0, "fixable": 0}`). A warning keyed on a runtime float's magnitude has no function/constant/syntax availability fact for PHPCompatibility's sniffs to detect, so this is the structural blindness the catalog's Backward Incompatible Changes rules generally run into this round, not an oversight in the mapping; `verification.phpcompatibility` is intentionally empty rather than guessed.

Evidence: UPGRADING-8.5.0, "1. Backward Incompatible Changes" -> Core: "A warning is now emitted when casting floats (or strings that look like floats) to int if they cannot be represented as one. This affects explicit int casts and implicit int casts." RFC: https://wiki.php.net/rfc/warnings-php-8-5#casting_out_of_range_floats_to_int -- and, immediately following it in the same list: "A warning is now emitted when casting NAN to other types." RFC: https://wiki.php.net/rfc/warnings-php-8-5#coercing_nan_to_other_types
